title: Heavy Computation: Web Workers & Pure Pipes

questions.prompt: What problem do Web Workers solve in an Angular app?

options.text: They make pipes re-run less often
They move CPU-intensive work off the main thread so the UI stays responsive
They give components access to a second DOM

questions.explanation: Workers run on a separate thread, so long computations don't freeze rendering, animations, or input on the main thread.

questions.prompt: How do the main thread and a worker exchange data?

options.text: Through message passing (postMessage/onmessage); data is copied via structured clone

questions.explanation: Workers are isolated — they communicate only by copied (or transferred) messages, never shared references.

questions.prompt: When does a pure pipe's transform() method re-run?

options.text: Only when a primitive input changes value, or an object/array input changes by reference
Only once, when the component is created
Whenever any signal in the app changes

questions.explanation: Pure pipes memoize by reference/value equality and reuse the cached output otherwise.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't a pure pipe re-run after array.push(item)?

options.text: push() mutates in place, so the array reference stays the same and the pipe sees no change

questions.explanation: Create a new reference instead, e.g. items.set([...items(), item]), so the reference-equality check detects the change.

questions.prompt: What must you always do with a worker you no longer need?

options.text: Call worker.terminate() (on completion, on error, and on destroy)

questions.explanation: An un-terminated worker keeps running in the background; use DestroyRef.onDestroy() as a safety net too.

questions.prompt: Which signal API offers the same lazy, memoized derivation as a pure pipe but works anywhere in TypeScript, not just templates?
questions.explanation: computed() recomputes only when a dependency changes and caches its result, usable throughout component logic.
